intro: Cardiff's seven mapped trees are mostly in Bute Park, where one short walk passes three Glamorgan champions, the Blackfriars plane at 612 centimetres round, a Turkey oak and a ginkgo that turns gold in November, plus a 34-metre beech. A sweet chestnut there sat unrecorded until volunteers taped it in 2023. Further out, the Maiden Oak of St Fagans, never pollarded, is put at 180 to 350 years, and a tree planted in 1985 remembers Raoul Wallenberg.
meta_description: Seven Cardiff trees: Bute Park's champion plane, Turkey oak and ginkgo, a 34m beech, the Maiden Oak of St Fagans and a Wallenberg memorial.
question_meta: Cardiff's oldest mapped tree is the Maiden Oak of St Fagans, estimated at 180 to 350 years old from its girth.
question_answer: Cardiff's oldest mapped tree is the Maiden Oak of St Fagans, estimated at 180 to 350 years old from its girth, standing uncut and unpollarded on the grounds of St Fagans National Museum of History.
question_context: Most of Britain's big old oaks were worked for a living, pollarded for firewood or cut back for fence posts, which squatted them and, as it turned out, kept them alive for centuries. This one was left alone. A maiden oak has never been cut, so what survives is the tree's own natural shape on a single trunk, now 5.38 metres round. Nobody has dated it directly. Put that girth through the usual rough growth rate for an open-grown oak, somewhere between one and a half and three centimetres a year, and the result is a band of roughly 180 to 350 years, which is as close as honesty gets without a corer. That range reaches back to somewhere between the reign of Charles II and the early years of Victoria's, meaning the tree was already standing well before the museum around it existed. Volunteers surveying Cardiff's ancient and veteran trees in 2023 updated its record rather than opening one; the inventories already knew about it. It stands among the farmhouses, chapels and cottages St Fagans has moved here piece by piece from across Wales.

faq.q: How old is the Maiden Oak of St Fagans?
faq.a: An estimated 180 to 350 years, derived from its 5.38-metre girth using the usual growth-rate calculation for an open-grown oak; nobody has dated it directly.

faq.q: What makes the Bute Park plane a 'champion' tree?
faq.a: It was measured at 612 centimetres round and 24 metres tall and recorded as the Glamorgan Champion London plane in 2022, the largest of its kind found in the county.

faq.q: Why is there a tree for Raoul Wallenberg in Cardiff?
faq.a: It was planted in 1985 to commemorate the Swedish diplomat who saved tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews in Budapest in 1944 before vanishing into Soviet custody; a plaque at its foot names him.

faq.q: Are all four Cardiff trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. St Fagans National Museum of History and Bute Park are both free, and Alexandra Gardens in Cathays Park, where the Wallenberg tree stands, is a public civic garden.

trees.name: The Raoul Wallenberg Tree

location.address: Alexandra Gardens, Cathays Park civic centre, Cardiff

trees.access: Free. Public civic garden in Cardiff's Cathays Park, home to the Welsh National War Memorial and several other memorials.
trees.transport: Central Cardiff, a few minutes' walk from Cardiff Central and Cardiff Queen Street stations.
trees.story:
Cardiff's memorial to a man who saved tens of thousands of lives is alive itself. It was planted in 1985 for Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who spent the last months of 1944 in Budapest issuing protective passports and running safe houses that kept Hungarian Jews off the deportation trains. In January 1945 Soviet forces took him into custody. He was never seen again, and what happened to him has never been established.

The tree stands in Alexandra Gardens in Cathays Park, the formal green rectangle at the centre of Cardiff's civic quarter, where the Welsh National War Memorial and a row of other monuments face each other across the grass. A plaque at its foot carries his name. Most of what is commemorated in that garden is carved; this is the one that has put on forty years of growth since it was dedicated.

It is young by the standards of this map, and it is here for what it stands for rather than for its age. It is a tree of heaven, a fast-growing species from China with long leaves made of many paired leaflets. No source places it more precisely than the garden, but Alexandra Gardens is small enough that you will find a tree with a Wallenberg plaque without much hunting.
trees.how_to_recognise: A tree of heaven with long leaves of many paired leaflets and a plaque at its foot naming Raoul Wallenberg, in Alexandra Gardens by the Welsh National War Memorial.
trees.verify_notes: 2026-10-16: species Ailanthus altissima, given by email by a Cardiff parks project and operational delivery officer (the ground's manager); the page had asked readers for the species.

trees.name: The Bute Park Sweet Chestnut
trees.age_estimate: veteran tree, exact age not documented

location.address: Bute Park, Cardiff (exact position within the park's 56 hectares not confirmed this pass)

trees.access: Free. Bute Park is Cardiff's largest and most central public park, immediately behind Cardiff Castle, open daily.
trees.transport: Central Cardiff, a short walk from Cardiff Castle and the city centre.
trees.story:
Bute Park holds more than 3,000 catalogued trees and 50 British champions, and it took until 2023 for anyone to formally record this sweet chestnut as a veteran. Volunteers from Coed Caerdydd and Coed Cadw, the Woodland Trust in Wales, measured it during Ancient Tree Inventory training days that year, with park staff member Nigel Pugh running the tape around the trunk: 4.7 metres. One of the most thoroughly surveyed municipal parks in Britain had a tree that size sitting outside its own records.

Sweet chestnut is not a British native. It came from the Mediterranean and went into estate grounds for its nuts, its timber and its looks, and old ones give themselves away: the bark twists into long spirals up the trunk as the tree ages, so a veteran looks as though someone has wrung it out. This one grows in the park immediately behind Cardiff Castle, free and open daily, on ground the city has had the run of for generations.

Two things we cannot give you. Nobody has dated it, so its age is not estimated but simply unrecorded, and the 4.7 metres remains the only hard number published about it. And nobody has said where in the park's 56 hectares it stands, so the pin marks the park rather than the trunk. If you find it, tell us where it is.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.7 metres round, and by the spiralling bark of an old sweet chestnut. It stands somewhere in Bute Park, behind Cardiff Castle; nobody has published exactly where.

best_time.label: October, when the spiny burrs split and the chestnuts come down

trees.name: The Maiden Oak of St Fagans
trees.species: Oak (Quercus, species not established -- likely Pedunculate Oak, Quercus robur, common in this region, not confirmed by a source)
trees.age_estimate: several hundred years, estimated from girth

location.address: St Fagans National Museum of History grounds, St Fagans

trees.access: Free. St Fagans National Museum of History is a major open-air museum on the western edge of Cardiff with free entry to the grounds and museum.
trees.transport: Western Cardiff, St Fagans; served by Cardiff Bus routes from the city centre, roughly 25-30 minutes.
trees.story:
Most of Britain's big old oaks were worked for a living. They were pollarded for firewood or cut back for fence posts, which squatted them and, as it turned out, kept them alive for centuries. This one was left alone. A maiden oak has never been cut, so what you get is the tree's own natural shape on a single trunk, and this trunk now measures 5.38 metres round on the grounds of St Fagans National Museum of History, on the western edge of Cardiff.

Nobody has dated it. Put the girth through the usual rough growth rate for an open-grown oak, somewhere between one and a half and three centimetres of girth a year, and you get a band of roughly 180 to 350 years, which is as close as honesty gets without a corer. That puts its first decades somewhere between the reign of Charles II and the early years of Victoria's, and it means the tree was already standing well before the museum was.

Volunteers surveying Cardiff's ancient and veteran trees in 2023 updated its record rather than opening one, so the inventories already knew about it. It stands among the farmhouses, chapels and cottages that St Fagans has moved here piece by piece from across Wales and rebuilt. The grounds are free. Nobody has published where in the 100 acres it stands, so allow time for the hunt.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its maiden form, one uncut trunk 5.38 metres round where most veteran oaks were pollarded centuries ago. It stands in the grounds of St Fagans National Museum of History, among the rebuilt Welsh buildings.

trees.name: The Blackfriars Champion Plane
trees.age_estimate: roughly 255 to 310 years, derived from girth (measured 2022)

location.address: South east edge of the Blackfriars site, Bute Park, Cardiff (OS grid ST 17804 76667)

trees.access: Free. Bute Park is Cardiff's largest and most central public park, immediately behind Cardiff Castle, open daily. Marked on site by a blue Champion Tree Trail plaque.
trees.transport: Central Cardiff, Bute Park, a short walk from Cardiff Castle and the city centre.
trees.story:
Bute Park has fifty British-champion trees and more than 3,000 catalogued specimens, and this London plane earned its own designation in 2022: Glamorgan Champion, the largest of its kind recorded in the county. It stands at the south east edge of the Blackfriars site, where a medieval friary once stood before the Bute family's landscaping buried its footprint under lawn.

The tree measures 612 centimetres round and 24 metres tall. Working backward from that girth using the standard method for estimating veteran trees in Britain, its age comes out at roughly 251 years on a good growing site or 307 on an average one, which would put its planting between 1715 and 1771. Either way it predates Andrew Pettigrew, who took up his post as head gardener to the third Marquis of Bute in 1873 and planted the avenues seen in the park today; nobody has found a record of who planted this one or when.

The date range reaches back to the mid eighteenth century, when the first Marquis employed Capability Brown to landscape the Castle Green nearby, and Cardiff's own parks record says London planes near Blackfriars may date from that work. No source ties this specific tree to Brown by name, so treat the connection as circumstantial rather than settled.

A blue plaque on the Champion Tree Trail marks it in the park.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its girth, 612 centimetres round, and a blue Champion Tree Trail plaque naming it Glamorgan Champion. It stands at the south east edge of the Blackfriars site in Bute Park, behind the castle.

trees.name: Old Man's Wood Beech, Bute Park

location.address: East edge of Old Man's Wood west, just north of the Blackfriars site, Bute Park, Cardiff CF10 3ER

trees.story:
The wood this beech stands in was scrub on an Ordnance Survey plan of 1851. As late as 1824, Old Man's Wood did not exist at all. The beech on its eastern edge is now 34 metres tall and was measured at 4.58 metres round in 2023, up from 4.33 seven years earlier.

Bute Park's own tree survey tries to date it from that girth and lands on two answers. If it grew on a good flood-plain site, it started around 1845. If its ground was only average, around 1768. The earlier date would make the tree older than the wood that now surrounds it; the later one would make it roughly the wood's own age. The survey does not choose between them, and neither do we.

Either way, it came up on the private grounds of Cardiff Castle, on the flood plain of the Taff, and it has kept growing through everything since, including the decades in which those grounds became a public park. Its neighbours make the walk. The Blackfriars plane, Glamorgan's champion London plane, stands about a hundred metres south, and a second big plane beside it, so the three make one short stop rather than three separate trips.

The tag on the trunk is a black plastic plate and hard to read, so do not count on it. Look up instead. At 34 metres it is easier to find by its crown than its label, and in late October that crown turns copper.

trees.name: Coopers Field Turkey Oak, Bute Park

location.address: North end of Coopers Field, Bute Park, Cardiff

trees.story:
Between 2016 and 2023 this oak put on 27 centimetres of girth, close to four centimetres a year, which is the growth of a tree nowhere near finished. It is already the champion Turkey oak of Glamorgan, named in 2023 as the largest of its kind recorded in the county, 33 metres tall and 4.13 metres round.

Turkey oaks are not native here. They come from southern Europe and Asia Minor, and they grow faster than Britain's own oaks. The bark gives it away, mauve-grey and broken into squarish plates, quite unlike the deep furrows of a pedunculate oak.

How it got to Coopers Field is not on record. Andrew Pettigrew, head gardener to the third Marquess of Bute from 1873, laid out circular beds featuring Turkey oaks in this park, and it would be tidy to say this is one of his. No source says so, and the park's own survey gives the tree no age at all. If you know when it went in, tell us.

What is certain is the setting. The oak stands at the northern end of Coopers Field by the canal side, a short walk from Cardiff Castle and the city centre. It is one of several county champions within a few minutes of each other in Bute Park, which makes an afternoon here a walk from record to record.

trees.name: Sunken Lawn Ginkgo, Bute Park

location.address: North east side of the Sunken Lawn, 63 m north west of Fishers Bridge, Bute Park, Cardiff

trees.story:
For a few days each November this tree turns the north-east side of the Sunken Lawn gold, then drops every leaf at once. It is Glamorgan's champion ginkgo, recorded in 2015 as the largest in the county and still growing hard. Its girth went from 3.02 metres in 2015 to 3.36 metres in 2023, and it stands 22 metres tall.

Ginkgo is the last survivor of a family of trees that was already ancient when the dinosaurs were alive. It was wild in only a few corners of China by the time temple gardeners there and in Japan took it up, and it reached European gardens in the 18th century. Bute Park has a whole avenue of them running from the castle to the Mews. This one stands apart from that avenue, near Fishers Bridge.

The park's survey records its size but not its age, and no planting date has turned up. If you know when it went in, tell us.

The rest of the year it is easy to walk past, a tall, upright crown of fan-shaped leaves on an ordinary lawn. Come in November instead. The gold lasts a short time, and when the leaves come down they come down nearly together, leaving a yellow circle on the grass around the trunk.

trees.name: Bute Park Wellingtonia

location.address: Blackweir woodland north, Bute Park, Cardiff

trees.story:
The world's largest tree species by volume has an outpost at the quiet end of Cardiff's main park. This giant sequoia stands in the Blackweir woodland at the far northern end of Bute Park, a long walk from the castle and the crowds, and it was measured in August 2016 at 25 metres tall with a trunk 472 centimetres round.

In California's Sierra Nevada the species grows to more than 80 metres and lives for thousands of years. Britain first saw it in 1853, when seed reached the country and Victorian gardeners fell for it, naming it Wellingtonia after the Duke of Wellington, who had died the year before. Planting one became the mark of a serious garden, which is why so many British parks and country houses still have a single soft, red-barked giant somewhere in the grounds.

This one is not a record. The park's champion tree table lists it without a champion title, and its figures are a decade old, so it has had ten more growing seasons than the numbers show. What it offers is the species itself, already broad in the trunk and still young by sequoia standards, and a reason to walk the full length of Bute Park instead of stopping at the castle end. Allow about 40 minutes on foot from Cardiff Central.

No source gives a planting date or an age. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the soft, red-brown bark of a giant sequoia on a trunk 472 centimetres round. It stands in the Blackweir woodland at the far northern end of Bute Park.

trees.name: Insole Court Cedar of Lebanon

location.address: South-west Lawn, Insole Court gardens, Fairwater Road, Llandaff, Cardiff CF5 2LN

official_register.name: Insole Court tree table, Glamorgan Champion 2005 (cardiffparks.org.uk, ref 184)

trees.access: Free: Insole Court gardens are a municipal park open to the public (Parks and Gardens UK record); the Welsh register lists the gardens Grade II*. Opening hours not checked, confirm at insolecourt.org.
trees.transport: Llandaff station about 20 minutes on foot; Cardiff Central about 10 minutes by bus then a short walk (not checked, confirm locally).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the large cedar on the South-west Lawn, its trunk 6.62 metres round. It stands just east of the corner steps that lead down from the Front Lawn below the house.
trees.story:
Measured by its trunk alone, this cedar would be older than the house it stands below. Cardiff's tree survey says as much, and then settles on a more modest answer.

The trunk was 6.62 metres round at one metre up in November 2024, up from 6.37 metres in 2017, and the tree has climbed from 20 to 22 metres in under a decade. On a good site, the survey notes, a girth like that suggests an age well beyond the property's. Its judgement is that it is probably safe to say the cedar went in around the time the first section of the gardens was laid out, in the early 1860s. That is the surveyor's reasoning rather than a dated planting record, and it gives the tree somewhere between 140 and 200 years.

Insole Court is a Victorian house built for the Insole family, now run by a community trust, with its grounds kept as a public park. The cedar has seen the place pass from a family's garden to everyone's, and in 2005 it was named the Glamorgan champion of its species.

It stands on the South-west Lawn, just east of the corner steps that lead down from the Front Lawn below the house, between two terraced lawns. The gardens are listed Grade II* on the Welsh register of historic parks and gardens. The community garden and stable yard are closed to visitors, but the lawns where the cedar grows are open.

trees.name: Cathays Cemetery Deodar

location.address: Immediately behind the chapels, Cathays Cemetery, Fairoak Road, Cardiff CF24 4PY

official_register.name: Cathays Cemetery tree table (cardiffparks.org.uk, tag 02410, ref 603)

trees.access: Free: Cathays Cemetery is an open public cemetery (Cadw register entry for the site; hours not checked).
trees.transport: Cathays station about 12 minutes on foot (not checked, confirm locally); Cardiff Queen Street about 20 minutes on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the round bed ringed by tarmac it grows in, and by the gap where a major limb came off its north-east side in 2026. It stands directly behind the twin chapels.
trees.story:
For most of its life this cedar went by the wrong name. Cardiff's tree records long called it a Cedar of Lebanon, until the surveyor measured its needles, 2 to 3.6 centimetres long, and found a deodar, the Himalayan cedar.

It stands in a round bed ringed by tarmac directly behind the twin chapels of Cathays Cemetery, which opened in 1859. The survey puts the tree at about 163 years old in 2020, working from a trunk 4.28 metres round just above the ground, and says that age is consistent with planting when the cemetery was laid out. That is the survey's reasoning rather than a planting record, so the range stays broad, somewhere between 140 and 190 years.

If the survey is right, the deodar has stood behind those chapels for almost the whole life of the cemetery, through a century and a half of Cardiff burying its dead. At 16 metres it is not tall. What it has is the spot.

It has not come through untouched. In 2026 it lost a major limb on its north-east side, and the gap is now part of how you will know it. The identification rests on that one survey, so treat it as the surveyor's call. If you know your cedars and disagree, tell us.

While you are here, follow the curving path north-west of the chapels to an Austrian pine, 4.10 metres round and 21 metres tall, the Glamorgan champion of its kind in 2020.

trees.name: Sunken Lawn Dawn Redwood, Bute Park

location.address: South edge of the Sunken Lawn, Bute Park, Cardiff CF10 3ER

official_register.name: Bute Park tree table, TROBI Remarkable Tree 2023 (cardiffparks.org.uk, tag 2310, ref 224)

trees.access: Free, open public park (Bute Park, 7:30am to 5:30pm per bute-park.com).
trees.transport: Cardiff Queen Street about 15 minutes on foot; Cardiff Central about 20 minutes.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fluted, buttressed red-brown trunk and soft feathery needles, which turn rust-orange and drop in autumn. It stands on the south edge of the Sunken Lawn, 25 metres tall.
trees.story:
This tree belongs to a species science only met alive in 1948. The dawn redwood was known from fossils before it was described from living trees in China that year, so whoever planted this one in Bute Park did it within the last eighty years at most.

It has made good use of the time. When the park's tree survey measured it in November 2015 the trunk was 2.70 metres round. By March 2023 it was 3.22 metres, more than half a metre added in under eight years, and the crown had reached 25 metres. That same year the Tree Register listed it as a Remarkable Tree.

It stands on the south edge of the Sunken Lawn, a short walk across the grass from the Sunken Lawn ginkgo. The trunk is red-brown, fluted and buttressed at the foot, and the needles are soft and feathery. It is a conifer that behaves like an oak. In autumn the needles turn rust-orange and fall, and all winter the tree stands bare.

What it lacks is a birthday. Nobody has recorded when it went into the ground, and the survey gives no planting date. If you know, or remember this lawn when the redwood was small, tell us.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn rust-orange before they fall

trees.name: Roath Park Lake Pedunculate Oak

location.address: East side of Roath Park Lake, almost opposite Lakeside Drive, Lake Road East, Cardiff CF23 5PA

official_register.name: Roath Park Lake tree table (cardiffparks.org.uk, ref 081)

trees.access: Free, open public park (Roath Park lakeside path, Lake Road East).
trees.transport: Cardiff Queen Street about 25 minutes by bus then a short walk (not checked, confirm locally); Roath Park lake is a well-served bus area.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad trunk, 3.44 metres round, under a low crown only 14 metres tall. It stands on the lakeside path on the east shore of Roath Park Lake, almost opposite Lakeside Drive.
trees.story:
This oak was on the map before the park was. Ordnance Survey sheets of 1880 and 1900 both show an oak at this spot on the east side of what is now Roath Park Lake, so it was already growing when the marshland here was made into a park.

Cardiff's tree survey measured it in January 2015 at 3.44 metres round and only 14 metres tall, a short, broad tree rather than a tall one. From that girth the survey works out about 173 years on an average site, or about 157 on a good one, which puts its start somewhere between the early 1840s and the late 1850s. Add the years since, and it is roughly 170 to 190 years old now. That is an estimate from size, not a planting record.

Either way, it has watched the marsh around it turn into a lake and a public park, and the park fill up with remarkable trees. By the count of the council's park site, Roath Park now holds the second largest number of champion trees of any public park in the UK.

This oak is not the grandest of them. It stands on a busy lakeside footpath beside Lake Road East, almost opposite Lakeside Drive, a modest tree with a long memory. The figures are from 2015, so it will have put on a few centimetres since. If you measure it, tell us.

trees.name: The Nursery Lawn Tulip Tree, Bute Park

location.address: East side of the Nursery Lawn, Bute Park, Cardiff CF10 3ER

trees.story:
Two record trees stand about 25 metres apart beside Bute Park's Sunken Lawn. One is Glamorgan's champion ginkgo. The other is this tulip tree, listed in 2023 as the champion for all of Wales, 29 metres tall and 4.68 metres round when it was measured in March 2022.

The tulip tree is a North American species, and this one flowers in June and July. The leaves are the easier clue from the ground, saddle-shaped, as if someone had taken the tip off each one with scissors. In autumn they turn yellow and gold.

The title rests on a single survey, made for the Tree Register and published on the park's own pages, and those pages give two addresses for it. The table says north-east of the Sunken Lawn. The tree's own page says the east side of the Nursery Lawn. The grid reference puts both descriptions on the same patch of ground, just south of the ginkgo.

What the survey does not give is an age. Nobody has recorded when this tree went in, so it stands here on its size alone. If you know the planting date, tell us.

Bute Park counts 51 champion trees in all, so this is one stop among many on an afternoon's walk behind Cardiff Castle.
